name: Treaty with the Potawatomi Nation, 1846
aka: Potawatomi Treaty of 1846 (Council Bluffs and Osage River)
nations: Potawatomi Nation (Bodéwadmi): the United Nation of Council Bluffs and the bands on the Osage River (today the Citizen Potawatomi Nation and the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation)
promises: Peace and friendship forever, with the United States promising all proper care and parental protection (Article 1).
$850,000 for the cession of the Iowa and Osage River lands, subject to the deductions in later articles (Article 3).

Possession and title to a thirty-mile-square tract of 576,000 acres on both sides of the Kansas River, with a guarantee of full and complete possession as the Nation's land and home forever, for which the Potawatomi paid $87,000 out of the $850,000 (Article 4).
The balance of the $850,000 held in trust at 5 percent interest (Article 7).

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission valued the Iowa tract and the Osage River tract ceded by this treaty at $4,341,217 in all (the Osage River tract at $591,217), found the Potawatomi were paid $1,051,000, less than one-fourth of the value, and held the consideration unconscionable.

breaches.what: The Commission found that the Act of 1 July 1862 granted a railroad right of way through the Kansas reservation this treaty guaranteed, appropriating 1,454.65 acres of Potawatomi land without the tribe's consent or any payment, and that the tribe was entitled to just compensation. A final award of $4,363.95 with interest from 1 July 1862 followed on 8 August 1955.

landTaken: The Potawatomi lands at Council Bluffs, Iowa, and on the Osage River, Kansas (Royce Areas 265 and 266), ceded by this treaty; and 1,454.65 acres of the new Kansas River reservation taken for the railroad in 1862 (Commission findings).
compensation: Consideration of $1,051,000 for the 1846 cession (1956 opinion). The 1959 final award in Dockets 15-J and 71-A is in the collection, but its scan is not legible enough to quote the amount. Railroad taking: $4,363.95 with interest (1955 final award).
today: The Kansas River reservation was later divided by the treaties of 1861 and 1867, and the Citizen Band moved to Indian Territory.

plain.promised: $850,000 for the Iowa and Osage River lands, and a 576,000-acre tract on the Kansas River guaranteed as the Nation's land and home forever, for which the Potawatomi paid $87,000 of that sum.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1956 that the Potawatomi were paid $1,051,000, less than one-fourth of the land's value, an unconscionable consideration. It also found an 1862 railroad grant took 1,454.65 acres of the guaranteed reservation without payment.
plain.today: The 1959 final award amount is not legible in the scan. A 1955 award of $4,363.95 with interest covered the railroad land. Whether either was paid has not been traced.

nationVoice.summary: The Nation recalls that in 1846 all the Potawatomi west of the Mississippi were moved onto one Kansas River reservation they were promised as their home, and that the later treaties were not applied as written, costing many members their land.

openQuestions: The net award in Dockets 15-J and 71-A is printed illegibly in the scans ($3,29?,217); read the 1959 final award in a clean copy before quoting a figure.
The Commission's ruling on the railroad taking rests on the Act of 1 July 1862 (12 Stat. 489), which was not opened directly.
The treaty was signed on 5 June 1846 at Council Bluffs and 17 June 1846 on the Osage River; the later date is used as signed.

Audit 2026-11-08: Article 4 promise now records the $87,000 the Potawatomi paid for the Kansas tract, which the 1956 findings use in arriving at the $1,051,000 consideration. Other figures (4,341,217; 591,217; 1,051,000; 1,454.65 acres; $4,363.95 with interest at 5% from July 1, 1862 to November 9, 1934 and 4% after) checked and held.
